title: Team plans, and work packages as sets of user stories
blurb: Explain how a work package becomes a set of user stories agreed between the project manager and product owner, and how the team turns it into an iteration-level team plan.
question: A project manager wants to hand the next piece of work to a delivery team. What form does the work package description take in PRINCE2 Agile, who agrees it, and who then plans the tasks?

teach.h: Two plans at the team level
teach.body: A work package description gives the information needed to deliver one or more products: activities, resources, product descriptions and constraints. In PRINCE2 Agile it is usually a set of user stories. A team plan is produced by the delivery team when it accepts a work package: a detailed, task-level plan for the next iteration. In short, the work package says what to deliver; the team plan says how the team will do it this iteration.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 8.1 and Glossary

teach.h: Agreed between the PM and the product owner
teach.body: The project manager is the only role with direct authority over the product owner, who is a version of the team manager role. The PM and PO agree work as work package descriptions expressed as sets of user stories, within the tolerances and management approaches. The PO is then the only role with direct authority over delivery team members, who self-manage how the work gets done.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 7.3.1 and Table 7.2

steps.label: Authorize
steps.sub: PM co-creates the WPD with the PO and team

steps.label: Accept
steps.sub: team reviews stories and produces a team plan

steps.label: Review plan
steps.sub: PM reviews the team plan and authorizes work

steps.label: Execute
steps.sub: team delivers and updates its dashboard

steps.label: Complete
steps.sub: PM confirms the set of user stories was delivered

teach.h: Work package description versus team plan

teach.body: When accepting a work package, the team reviews the user stories, produces a team plan of what it can complete within the constraints, reviews risks, advises the PM and agrees to deliver. The plan is detailed only for the next iteration. The release map stays high level, so effort is not wasted planning tasks that may change.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 13.12 and 8.3.2.5

teach.h: Team planning workshop: building the team plan
head: Topic
What it achieves
rows: Clarify and prioritize stories with MoSCoW
Shared view of each story's effort
Select stories into a realistic team plan

teach.body: Kestrel is building a claims portal. Project manager Ruth Calloway and product owner Marcus Yeo agree a work package of six user stories for uploading photos of damage, with zero tolerance on time and cost and two Could-have stories that may drop. In the team planning workshop, Marcus's team refines the stories, estimates them and breaks the selected ones into tasks for the iteration. Ruth reviews the team plan and authorizes the work. At the end, she confirms which stories were delivered.

teach.text: The team plan is produced by the delivery team, not by the project manager or chief product owner. The work package description is agreed between the PM and the PO; it is not the product backlog itself, and it is not agreed with the CPO. Team plans cover the next iteration; the release map covers releases and stages.

items: Work package description in agile: usually a set of user stories.
Agreed between the project manager and the product owner, within tolerances.
The PO is a version of the team manager role.
Team plan: produced by the delivery team when accepting a work package.
Team plan: detailed, task-level, for the next iteration only.
Built in the team planning workshop; iteration planning selects the stories.

summary: You can now explain that an agile work package description is a set of user stories agreed between the project manager and product owner. You can also describe the team plan as the delivery team's task-level plan for the next iteration, built in the team planning workshop.

A.q: In PRINCE2 Agile, what form does a work package description usually take?
A.why: In agile, the work package description is expressed as a set of user stories (7.3.1, Table 8.1).

whyNot.0: The release map is the project and stage plan.
whyNot.1: The project canvas is the business case artifact.
whyNot.3: The team dashboard replaces the checkpoint report.

A.q: Who agrees a work package description in a PRINCE2 Agile project?
options: The project manager and product owner
The chief product owner and team coach
The project executive and project manager
The product owner and project support
A.why: The PM and PO agree work as work package descriptions, expressed as sets of user stories (7.3.1, Table 7.2).

whyNot.1: The CPO prioritizes across teams and the team coach supports self-management; neither agrees work packages.
whyNot.2: The executive is accountable for the project but does not agree team work packages.
whyNot.3: Project support gives administrative help; it does not agree work packages.

A.why: The team plan is produced by the delivery team when accepting a work package (Table 8.1).

whyNot.0: The PM reviews the team plan but does not produce it.
whyNot.1: The CPO owns the project backlog, not team plans.
whyNot.2: Project support helps with administration and dashboards, not team planning.

B.q: When is a team plan produced?
options: When the board authorizes the project
When the delivery team accepts a work package
When the project manager reports highlights
When the project reaches a stage boundary
B.why: The team plan is produced by the delivery team when it accepts a work package (Table 8.1, Table 13.12).

whyNot.0: Project authorization approves the PID; team plans come later, per work package.
whyNot.2: Reporting highlights updates the project dashboard.
whyNot.3: At a stage boundary the release map is updated; team plans are made per iteration.

B.q:
Which two statements about work packages and team plans are correct?
1. The chief product owner drafts a work package description for each team.
2. The team plan replaces the release map.
3. A team plan is a detailed, task-level plan for the next iteration.
4. The PM reviews the team plan when authorizing a work package.
B.why: Statements 3 and 4 are correct (Table 8.1, Table 13.9). Work packages are agreed by the PM and PO, and the release map remains the project and stage plan.

whyNot.0: Both are false: the PM and PO agree work packages, and the team plan does not replace the release map.
whyNot.1: Statement 1 is false: the CPO does not draft work package descriptions.
whyNot.2: Statement 2 is false: the release map remains the project and stage plan.

B.q: Identify the missing words in the following sentence. The [?] is the only role with direct authority over the product owner.
B.why: The project manager is the only role with direct authority over the product owner (7.3.1).

whyNot.1: The CPO works closely with POs on priorities but does not hold direct authority over them.
whyNot.2: The executive directs through the board, not directly over product owners.
whyNot.3: The team coach supports the team's self-management and has no authority over the PO.

C.q: In which workshop is the team plan built, and under which topic are stories selected for it?
options: Team planning workshop; user story refinement
C.why: The team planning workshop prepares the next iteration; iteration planning selects stories by priority and estimate into a realistic team plan (Table 13.13).

whyNot.0: Release planning updates the release map and team OKRs at a stage boundary.
whyNot.2: The workshop is right, but user story refinement clarifies acceptance criteria rather than selecting stories.
whyNot.3: The kickoff workshop sets up team dashboards, values and skills during initiation.

C.q: Which process includes the 'accept a work package' activity, and what does the team produce in it?
options: Controlling a stage; a team plan
Managing product delivery; a release map
Managing product delivery; a team plan
Controlling a stage; a work package description
C.why: 'Accept a work package' is in managing product delivery, where the team produces a team plan of what it can complete (Table 13.12).

whyNot.0: The product is right, but accepting a work package is a managing product delivery activity.
whyNot.1: The process is right, but the release map is the PM's project and stage plan.
whyNot.3: The WPD is agreed in 'authorize a work package' in controlling a stage; accepting it is the team's step.

C.q: In 'receive completed work package', what does the project manager confirm?
options: That the set of user stories was delivered
That the CPO has signed off the project canvas
That the release map has been replaced
That velocity matched the original estimate
C.why: Receiving a completed work package confirms that the set of user stories or timebox features was delivered (Table 13.9).

whyNot.1: Signing off the canvas is not part of receiving a work package.
whyNot.2: The release map is updated, not replaced, as work completes.
whyNot.3: Velocity is measured as evidence for forecasting, not checked against an original estimate here.

reteach.title: The order and the kitchen
reteach.question: In a restaurant, the waiter agrees the order with the head chef. Who then decides how the kitchen prepares each dish?

blocks.body: The work package is the order: a set of user stories the project manager agrees with the product owner. The team plan is the kitchen's plan: the team itself decides the tasks for the next iteration. The PM checks the plan and later confirms which stories were delivered.

blocks.text: The work package is agreed by the PM and PO; the team plan is made by the team.

explain.body: It gives the information to deliver one or more products: activities, resources, product descriptions and constraints. In agile it is usually a set of user stories.

test.q: A work package description gives the information needed to deliver one or more products. Which contents does it include?
test.why: The glossary describes it as information to deliver products: activities, resources, product descriptions and constraints.

whyNot.0: Benefits and options belong to the business case (project canvas).
whyNot.2: Risk details are recorded in the risk register.
whyNot.3: Lessons and causes are recorded in the lessons log and lessons report.

explain.body: The PO is a version of the team manager role, reports to the PM and agrees work packages with them.

test.q: Which role is described as a version of the team manager role?
test.why: The product owner is a version of the team manager role (7.3.1).

whyNot.0: The team coach helps one or two teams self-manage; it is not a management role.
whyNot.1: The CPO represents users and owns the project backlog.
whyNot.3: The agile coach works across the organization on systemic blockers.

explain.body: Topics: product backlog refinement, user story refinement, effort estimation and iteration planning, which produces the team plan.

test.q: Which topic of the team planning workshop selects stories by priority and estimate?
test.why: Iteration planning selects stories by priority and estimate into a realistic team plan (Table 13.13).

whyNot.0: Effort estimation builds a shared view of each story's effort before selection.
whyNot.1: Backlog refinement clarifies and prioritizes the backlog with MoSCoW.
whyNot.2: Story refinement makes acceptance criteria clear and testable.

explain.body: A team plan is a detailed, task-level plan covering the next iteration. The release map holds the higher-level view.

test.q: What horizon and level of detail does a team plan cover in PRINCE2 Agile?
options: The whole stage, at release level
The next iteration, at task level
The whole project, at epic level
The next release, at feature level
test.why: The team plan is a detailed task-level plan for the next iteration (Table 8.1).

whyNot.0: A stage-level view is the release map as stage plan.
whyNot.2: Project-level epics sit in the project backlog and release map.
whyNot.3: Releases and features are shown on the release map.
